enrichment.short_title: Class-based asylum risk and the gross-and-systematic test

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: A Syrian national appealed after the IAT dismissed his asylum and Article 3 claims relating to refusal of leave to enter as a refugee.
His personal case rested on a dispute over a third period of military service; the IAT found no individual risk of serious ill-treatment if returned.
On the remaining ground, he argued that as a failed asylum seeker, draft evader and unauthorised leaver he faced class-based persecution or Article 3 ill-treatment in Syria.
The IAT required evidence of a consistent pattern of gross and systematic violation of fundamental human rights before accepting such class-based risk.
Ward LJ granted permission on the single ground that this standard was inconsistent with the Sivakumaran real-risk test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission on one ground against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination dismissing asylum and Article 3 appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where an asylum or Article 3 claim depends entirely on risk as a member of a class rather than on facts personal to the claimant, the Sivakumaran 'real risk' standard logically requires proof that ill-treatment of the relevant kind generally or consistently occurs in the country of return; a tribunal may therefore properly require a consistent pattern of gross and systematic violation of fundamental human rights before finding class-based persecution or Article 3 ill-treatment, and that approach is an application of, not a departure from, the real-risk test.
legal_issues: Whether the gross-and-systematic human-rights standard is compatible with the Sivakumaran real-risk test
Whether class-based risk of ill-treatment for draft evaders and unauthorised leavers must be established without reference to personal circumstances
Whether the UN Convention Against Torture Article 3(2) approach may be applied to refugee and ECHR Article 3 claims
linked_authorities: Sivakumaran v Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Single-ground appeal with clear ratio on class-based risk and the real-risk standard; personal credibility findings were not renewed.

enrichment.short_title: Clinical negligence protocol breach and CFA success fee
key_facts: The claimant suffered injury when her child was delivered stillborn at Harold Wood Hospital in September 1997.
Proceedings were issued in September 2000, shortly before limitation expired, before a letter of claim was sent in December 2000.
The claim was funded by a CFA with a 100% success fee and ATE insurance from July 2000 after legal aid was refused.
The defendant eventually consented to judgment for damages to be assessed in February 2002.
The defendant applied to disallow or reduce the success fee and other costs for failure to comply with the Pre-Action Protocol for Clinical Disputes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs application after consent judgment in clinical negligence proceedings, alleging pre-action protocol non-compliance and misconduct under CPR 44.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no sanction imposed for failure to observe paragraph 3.21 of the Clinical Disputes Protocol.
enrichment.ratio: Non-compliance with the Pre-Action Protocol for Clinical Disputes does not justify a costs sanction where the innocent party was given ample time to investigate and defend, where it is unlikely the claim would have settled pre-issue even with full protocol compliance, and where funding arrangements and expert evidence reasonably delayed the letter of claim until shortly before protective issue was necessary to protect the limitation position.
legal_issues: Whether issuing before a letter of claim breached the Clinical Disputes Pre-Action Protocol
Whether the court should disallow or reduce a 100% CFA success fee for protocol non-compliance
Whether the defendant was prejudiced by extensions of time for service of defence
Application of Practice Direction (Pre-Action Protocols) sanctions
linked_authorities: Ricardo Biguzzi v Rank Leisure Plc

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural history and clear refusal of sanctions; Lord Woolf's reasoning on prejudice and settlement likelihood is explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Adjournment refused for late permission-to-appeal bundle
key_facts: Miss Hamid-Zadeh was evicted from her flat in February 2000 and pursued multiple sets of proceedings alleging conspiracy and improper eviction.
Master Eyre struck out her claim; Nelson J granted limited permission to appeal and Bell J partially reinstated claims against her landlady.
She lodged a notice of appeal on 9 December 2002 and sought an adjournment of the permission hearing because a transcript of Bell J's judgment was not yet available.
She had recently borrowed money to order the transcript and complained about summary assessment of costs at the Bell J hearing.
Master Venne had already refused an adjournment; Brooke LJ reconsidered the application as vacation business.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to the Court of Appeal to reconsider Master Venne's refusal to adjourn an application for permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application for adjournment refused; permission hearing to remain listed.
enrichment.ratio: An application for permission to appeal should not be adjourned at a very late stage because a litigant in person has only recently ordered a transcript and failed to prepare documents in good time after lodging notice of appeal months earlier; the judge hearing permission may consider any transcript if delivered urgently.
legal_issues: Whether to adjourn an application for permission to appeal for late transcript production
Whether a litigant in person should receive a three-judge court for a permission application
Propriety of summary costs assessment where the bill was not filed 24 hours before the hearing

confidence.notes: Procedural ruling only; underlying housing merits not decided. Judge metadata in source file is incomplete.

enrichment.short_title: Fair rent appeal on scarcity and comparables reasoning
key_facts: Wolters (London) Ltd appealed fair rent determinations for four regulated studio flats at 27 Lancaster Gate, W2.
The London Rent Assessment Committee used comparables within the same refurbished building and applied AST starting rents with deductions for physical differences and tenancy terms.
Grounds challenged the Committee's reasoning on starting points, physical adjustments, cigarette smoke stains, maintenance terms, and scarcity under section 70(2).
Harrison J upheld some grounds on inadequate reasoning regarding cigarette smoke stains, maintenance/decoration differences, and scarcity.
The Committee took Westminster, Camden and Kensington and Chelsea as the scarcity locality and applied a 20% scarcity deduction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 11(1) of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against London Rent Assessment Committee fair rent determinations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; determination quashed and remitted to a differently constituted committee; landlord awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: A rent assessment committee must give intelligible reasons for fair rent calculations under section 70 of the Rent Act 1977, including whether tenant-caused disrepair under section 70(3)(a) was disregarded, whether deductions reflect genuine tenancy-term differences, and whether a scarcity discount under section 70(2) is justified by reasons distinguishing amenity-driven demand from broad housing shortage over a sufficiently large locality explained with adequate reasoning for the percentage chosen.
legal_issues: Adequacy of reasons for adopting comparables as starting points under section 70(1)
Whether cigarette smoke stains were improperly deducted contrary to section 70(3)(a)
Whether a 10% deduction for regulated-tenancy terms was adequately reasoned
Appropriate geographic locality and reasoning for scarcity under section 70(2)
Adequacy of reasons for a 20% scarcity discount
index_terms: Curtis v London Rent Assessment Committee
linked_authorities: Metropolitan Property Holdings Ltd v Finegold
Curtis v London Rent Assessment Committee
Spath Holme Ltd v Chairman of the Greater Manchester Assessment Committee
Queensway Association v Chairman of the Chiltern, Thames and Eastern Rent Assessment Committee
Yeoman's Row Management Ltd v Chairman of the London Rent Assessment Committee

confidence.notes: Long judgment with detailed grounds analysis; some comparables reasoning upheld despite inadequacy concerns.

enrichment.short_title: Limited adjournment of defamation permission hearing
key_facts: Mr Mahajan brought a defamation claim after summary judgment was entered against him by Eady J.
He lodged a notice of appeal on 4 March 2003 and sought more time to prepare because of multiple concurrent litigation deadlines.
Master Venne refused adjournment of the permission hearing fixed for 5 June 2003.
Mahajan applied to Brooke LJ as vacation business, alleging unfairness and court corruption concerns.
Brooke LJ offered an alternative June date but Mahajan insisted he could not prepare during June.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to reconsider Master Venne's direction refusing adjournment of an application for permission to appeal in a defamation action.
enrichment.outcome: Application partially allowed; hearing removed from 5 June and refixed for 27 June with direction that a transcript of Brooke LJ's judgment be provided to the hearing judge.
enrichment.ratio: Courts must balance fairness to both sides and deal with permission applications promptly; where a litigant in person immediately objects to the first listed date but refuses any hearing within a reasonable period, a short refixing rather than indefinite adjournment may be appropriate, though excessive delay should not be permitted.
legal_issues: Whether to adjourn an application for permission to appeal for preparation time
Fairness to respondents in knowing whether an appeal will proceed
Management of multiple concurrent litigation by a litigant in person

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment with clear refixing order; defamation merits not addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Port-of-entry student refusal under Immigration Rules
key_facts: Mr Cassimkhan, a Mauritian national aged 28, arrived at Heathrow on 31 January 2003 seeking leave to enter as a student for two years.
He had been refused entry clearance at the British High Commission in Mauritius one month earlier on genuineness, intention to leave and means grounds.
He planned to study English at Richmond Adult Community College and then a motor technician diploma, having worked as a bus company electrician since leaving school at 16.
The immigration officer refused leave, finding he was not a genuine student who intended to leave after his studies.
Judicial review was brought on grounds relating to paragraph 57(ii), irrelevant considerations, and irrationality of the paragraph 57(iv) refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review with permission granted on the papers of a port-of-entry refusal of student leave.
enrichment.ratio: A port refusal expressed under Immigration Rules paragraph 57(iv) for lack of genuine intention to leave after studies is lawful where the officer's finding of fact on intention is supported by evidence including limited educational preparation, vague career plans, and prior entry clearance refusals; failure expressly to address paragraph 57(ii) does not vitiate the decision if the operative refusal rests on paragraph 57(iv), and non-refusal under paragraph 57(vi) does not mean means were accepted.
legal_issues: Whether the immigration officer failed to apply paragraph 57(ii) student course requirements
Whether previous entry clearance refusals were an irrelevant consideration
Whether refusal under paragraph 57(iv) was irrational given alleged satisfaction of paragraph 57(vi)
Lawfulness of a 'genuine student' finding ancillary to paragraph 57(iv)
index_terms: Secretary of State for the Home Department

confidence.notes: Grounds analysis is explicit; second ground not pursued at hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Planning enforcement on boat racks and fourth-tier storage
key_facts: Exmouth Marina Ltd appealed under section 289 against an inspector's decision upholding an enforcement notice requiring removal of boat racking built contrary to 2001 planning permission at Exmouth.
The racks as built were 8.3m high rather than the permitted 6.8m and included a fourth storage level on top.
The appellant conceded breach and sought modification under ground (f) rather than complete removal.
The inspector interpreted the permission as limiting storage to three levels within the racking framework, excluding boats on top.
Sullivan J held that interpretation strained the permission and that the inspector failed properly to address the ground (f) fallback.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 289 statutory challenge to a planning inspector's decision on an enforcement notice appeal under grounds (a) and (f), and a related costs decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; enforcement and costs decisions remitted to the Secretary of State; costs summarily assessed at £12,500; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A planning permission must clearly impose any limitation on use such as prohibiting boat storage on the top of permitted structures; condition requiring compliance with approved drawings cannot be strained to exclude fourth-tier storage where the application contemplated four boats stacked and the drawings do not prohibit top storage; on a ground (f) appeal where an appellant proposes identifiable modifications including reduced height and shortened rack length, an inspector must grapple with that fallback and cannot refuse amendment principally because of an erroneous view that top storage was unauthorised.
legal_issues: Construction of 2001 planning permission regarding fourth-level boat storage
Whether the inspector compared built racks with permitted racks on the correct basis
Whether the inspector adequately considered ground (f) modification proposals
Application of Taylor & Sons (Farms) to sufficiency of fallback material
Lawfulness of the inspector's costs decision
linked_authorities: Taylor & Sons (Farms) v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions

confidence.notes: Detailed planning merits and permission construction analysis; Taylor distinguished on facts.

enrichment.short_title: No main-contractor liability for Cliveden roof membrane
key_facts: The National Trust sued stone restorer Mr Mates for a failed roof waterproof membrane at Cliveden Mansion's East Curved Link, installed by Ajap using Grace materials in 1995.
The roof leaked in 1999; the Trust alleged Mr Mates was main contractor under IFC 84 terms and liable for Ajap's and Grace's defects.
Mr Mates performed limited ancillary works only, including removing old asphalt and temporary weatherproofing; Ajap was instructed by the architects via Mr Mates as agent.
The Trust could not produce a signed IFC 84 contract and witnesses could not recall an oral main-contract agreement at an alleged July 1995 meeting.
Preliminary issues were ordered on retainer terms, subcontracting, and liability for Ajap's and Grace's workmanship and materials.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues in TCC proceedings before full technical trial on responsibility of the first defendant stone restorer.
enrichment.outcome: Action against first defendant dismissed; claimant to pay costs on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: A party cannot be held liable as main contractor for specialist waterproofing works performed by an independent contractor where there is no credible evidence that he agreed to undertake the whole roofing project on main-contractor or IFC 84 terms; administrative services, payment of third-party invoices with a mark-up, and CDM questionnaire answers do not establish main-contractor status or vicarious liability for nominated specialists instructed by the employer's architect.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Mates was retained as main contractor for the East Curved Link roof works
Whether IFC 84 terms were incorporated by oral agreement, letters or course of dealing
Whether Mr Mates retained Ajap as subcontractor or acted as the Trust's agent
Liability for defective workmanship and materials of Ajap and Grace

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on contract formation; technical defect merits reserved for later trial if pursued against others.

enrichment.short_title: Extradition habeas corpus after Czech in-absentia conviction
key_facts: Stefan Togyer applied for habeas corpus after committal on bail by Bow Street Magistrates' Court pending extradition to the Czech Republic.
He was convicted in his absence and sentenced to ten months' imprisonment for a dishonesty offence involving theft of electrical goods worth about £40.
He had notice of proceedings, apologised for non-attendance at the main hearing, and a court-appointed lawyer represented him in inquisitorial proceedings.
He had serious prior convictions including a ten-year sentence and was on licence at the time of the offence.
He challenged return under section 6(2) as not in the interests of justice and under section 11(3)(a) as trivial and oppressive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application under section 11 of the Extradition Act 1989 following committal to await the Home Secretary's extradition decision.
enrichment.ratio: Extradition may proceed where the applicant was convicted in his absence but had notice of proceedings and deliberately absented himself, a lawyer was appointed in inquisitorial Czech proceedings, and the offence cannot be regarded as trivial given the applicant's serious criminal record and commission of the offence while on licence, even if the goods were of limited value.
legal_issues: Whether return would not be in the interests of justice under section 6(2) for an in-absentia conviction
Whether the offence was trivial under section 11(3)(a)
Whether Czech inquisitorial trial procedure rendered conviction unsafe
Relevance of prior convictions and being on licence to triviality

confidence.notes: Lord Chief Justice judgment with agreed facts on notice of proceedings; value of goods assumed for argument.

enrichment.short_title: Iran military desertion and Article 3 prison conditions
key_facts: An Iranian citizen claimed asylum in October 2000 citing family political activity and harsh military punishment including detention and beating.
The adjudicator found him not wholly credible, accepted two periods of detention, and held desertion would be prosecuted but not reach Article 3 severity.
Country reports described harsh Iranian prison conditions, torture and systematic human rights abuses.
The IAT refused leave to appeal; Lightman J granted limited permission to review whether prison conditions were properly considered.
Kay J held the adjudicator sufficiently addressed prison conditions and reasons in the round.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with limited permission of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal against an adjudicator's dismissal of asylum and human rights claims.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's determination on Article 3 need not exhaustively analyse every country report if read as a whole it shows consideration of prison conditions and explains why, given rejected political significance and accepted military-discipline prosecution, return is unlikely to involve treatment crossing the Article 3 threshold by duration or conditions; inadequate reasons challenges must not rewrite the determination.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator sufficiently considered general prison conditions in Iran
Adequacy of reasons for finding desertion punishment would not breach Article 3
Application of R v IAT ex parte Amin and English v Emery Reimbold principles to IAT determinations
Lawfulness of the IAT's refusal of leave to appeal
linked_authorities: R v Immigration Appeal Tribunal ex parte Amin
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd

confidence.notes: Limited permission scope; Kay J's reasons analysis is the core holding.
